title: Bidirectional BFS in Auckland: Meet in the Middle
description: Watch how Bidirectional BFS finds the fastest route by expanding search frontiers from both start and goal simultaneously. The visualization maps streets into a graph and stops as soon as the two waves meet.
ig_caption:
🚦✨ **Bidirectional BFS in Auckland (Ponsonby)** is pure “meet-in-the-middle” magic.

At a graph level, we model real streets as an **unweighted graph** (intersections = nodes, road segments = edges). Instead of running one BFS from the start, **Bidirectional BFS launches two BFS searches**—one forward from the start and one backward from the goal—then **terminates when the frontiers intersect**. 🎯

Why it’s powerful: with branching factor *b* and shortest path length *d*, classic BFS can explore ~**b^d** states, while bidirectional search often reduces this to about **2·b^(d/2)**, dramatically shrinking the visited area on dense street networks. 🧠🌐

In this visualization, notice how the expanding rings accelerate early and converge quickly when the solution becomes “provable.” 📍

fb_caption:
🗺️🧠 In this pathfinding reel, we use **Bidirectional BFS** to search Auckland’s streets like a graph: intersections become nodes, roads become edges. Instead of searching from start to goal in one direction, we expand from **both ends at once** and stop when the searches meet—making the route discovery much more efficient.

Share this with a friend who loves algorithms, and tell me: would you rather see A* or Dijkstra next?
yt_description:
Bidirectional BFS pathfinding visualization in a real city map (Auckland Ponsonby)! 🚦 In this Short, we convert street intersections to graph nodes and road segments to edges, then run **Bidirectional BFS** by expanding two BFS frontiers from start and goal until they meet. Perfect for learning graph search, unweighted shortest paths, frontier intersection, and why bidirectional search can reduce explored states dramatically.
